title: Philosophy of physics: space, time and quantum mechanics
audience: a college student in a philosophy degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Study what physics says about reality, with the mathematics it needs: absolute and relational space from Newton and Leibniz, the bucket argument, special relativity (spacetime diagrams, the relativity of simultaneity, time dilation and the twin paradox) and its bearing on the metaphysics of time, entropy and the direction of time, and quantum mechanics (states and probabilities, measurement, entanglement and Bell's theorem) with its main interpretations.
primary_reading: MIT OpenCourseWare 24.111 Philosophy of Quantum Mechanics (free)

weeks.1: Newton and Leibniz: absolute and relational space
weeks.2: The bucket argument and Galilean relativity
weeks.3: Special relativity: the postulates, simultaneity and spacetime diagrams
weeks.4: Time dilation, length contraction and the twin paradox
weeks.5: Relativity and the metaphysics of time: presentism and the block universe
weeks.6: Entropy and the direction of time
weeks.7: Quantum mechanics I: states, superposition and probabilities
weeks.8: Quantum mechanics II: measurement and the measurement problem
weeks.10: Bell's theorem and the CHSH inequality
weeks.12: Interpretations: QBism, relational views and what quantum mechanics says about reality

blocks.deliverable: Reconstruct the bucket argument and the relationist reply.
Compute time dilation and the ages of the twins.
Evaluate the argument from relativity against presentism.
Week 7 midterm; compute outcome probabilities for spin measurements.
Derive the CHSH bound and the quantum value.
Write a three-page comparison of two interpretations.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Interpretation report: choose two interpretations of quantum mechanics, explain how each answers the measurement problem using a worked example (a spin measurement or a Bell experiment), state what each says exists, compare their costs, and write a 2,500-word report that defends one or explains why the question remains open.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
